explanations: luna: The section's dictionary form explains dīn as judgment, accounting, and recompense; al-Fātiḥa names Allah as “مَٰلِكِ يَوْمِ الدِّينِ,” locating the account with its owner. | terra: مَٰلِكِ يَوْمِ ٱلدِّينِ names the owner of the day on which the section's open account is finally settled.

luna: This covenant passage joins kindness to orphans and the needy with prayer and zakāh, then says the people turned away; it bundles the very duties the section's actor refuses. | terra: The covenant commands worship of God alone, kindness to orphans and the needy, prayer, and zakāt before charging most addressees with turning away, a near-complete ledger of the source's relations.
terra: Prayer and zakāt are followed by the promise that whatever good people send ahead they will find with God, treating the paid social due as stored credit.
terra: Submitting one's face to God while doing good brings a wage with the Lord; this repeats the submission-and-recompense connection stated more explicitly elsewhere.
terra: Ibrahim answers the command “submit” with أَسْلَمْتُ لِرَبِّ ٱلْعَٰلَمِينَ, enacting the yieldedness identified as dīn's underlying root sense in the source.
terra: Ibrahim and Jacob charge their children to die only as submitters because God chose the dīn for them, explicitly joining dīn to islām.

luna: The section's orphan and poor are people whose share is refused; this account of righteousness includes giving wealth to relatives, orphans, the needy, and travelers, so righteousness is measured by what reaches them. | terra: Righteous dīn is made concrete by giving cherished wealth to relatives, orphans, the needy and traveler, establishing prayer and zakāt, and fulfilling covenants.
terra: The bequest for parents and relatives is described as a prescribed fair duty, another human claim entered before an estate closes.
terra: The ban on consuming one another's wealth falsely or using judges to take it knowingly protects the two-sided human account from legal manipulation.

luna: The section preserves the dictionary idiom كذب عليكم الحج as meaning Hajj became incumbent; this ayah commands, “أَتِمُّوا الْحَجَّ وَالْعُمْرَةَ لِلَّهِ,” making the obligation's object explicit.
terra: Each receives a share of what was earned and God is swift in account, stating both the booked portion and its prompt settlement.
terra: Reform of the orphans' affairs is best; if property is mixed, they are brothers, and God knows the corrupter from the reformer, guarding the claimant behind the account.
terra: A divorced woman is to receive a fair gift according to the giver's means, حَقًّا عَلَى ٱلْمُحْسِنِينَ; ability affects amount, not the obligation to give.
terra: Divorced women receive a fair provision حَقًّا عَلَى ٱلْمُتَّقِينَ, making a material kindness an owed right.

luna: The section develops literal borrowing and repayment as an image for divine recompense; this ayah asks who will lend Allah a good loan for multiplication, turning the debt relation toward generous giving. | terra: A “good loan” to God is multiplied many times; voluntary giving is pictured as a debt whose supreme payer never withholds repayment.
terra: Believers are told to spend from divine provision before a day with no bargaining, friendship, or intercession; the opportunity to pay the social due has a closing date.
terra: لَآ إِكْرَاهَ فِى ٱلدِّينِ is a necessary boundary on the source dictionary's “submission” sense: dīn is not produced by human compulsion.
terra: Wealth spent in God's way is multiplied like one seed yielding seven hundred, making a given amount a credit repaid far beyond its face value.

luna: The section's prayer-and-charity portrait includes “يُرَاءُونَ”; this ayah warns that spending for show, “رِئَاءَ النَّاسِ,” can void charity, exposing the opposite of giving as a true due. | terra: Charity is nullified by reproach, injury, and spending to be seen while disbelieving in God and the Last Day; a visible payment can therefore be absent from the true account.
terra: Givers must not select defective goods that they themselves would accept only with closed eyes, defining a real payment rather than token disposal.
terra: Satan promises poverty while God promises forgiveness and bounty, exposing the fear of loss that turns received good into withholding.

luna: The section's surah condemns prayer and deeds performed to be seen; this ayah says public charity is good, but concealing it while giving to the poor is better, distinguishing visible performance from actual aid. | terra: Concealed charity to the poor is better for the giver, supplying the opposite of a visible religious act detached from a true payment.
terra: Whatever good people spend is for themselves and يُوَفَّ إِلَيْكُمْ in full without wrong, turning charity into a precisely repaid credit.
terra: The restrained poor are mistaken for self-sufficient because they do not beg insistently; this identifies the hidden creditor whose share must not depend on asking.
terra: Those who spend by night and day, secretly and openly, have their wage with their Lord; continuous giving answers both withholding and concern for display.
terra: Faith, good works, prayer, and zakāt receive their wage with the Lord, joining obedience and material payment to recompense.
terra: Repentant creditors retain only their principal: لَا تَظْلِمُونَ وَلَا تُظْلَمُونَ defines settlement as neither taking another's right nor losing one's own.

luna: Where the section shows dues refused to the orphan and poor, this ayah requires leniency toward a debtor in hardship and says remission is better, reversing the withholding posture. | terra: A debtor in hardship receives delay, and remitting the debt as charity is better; the ayah sets mercy within, rather than outside, the creditor-debtor account.

luna: The section's account is a debt that must be paid; this ayah warns of the day each soul is returned to Allah and fully paid for what it earned, without injustice. | terra: Immediately before the written-debt ayah, every soul is returned to God and paid in full for what it earned without injustice, joining the earthly ledger to its final closure.

luna: The section's dictionary form داينت names giving or taking a debt; “إِذَا تَدَايَنتُم بِدَيْنٍ ... فَاكْتُبُوهُ” gives the literal written debt ledger behind that image. | terra: The debt ayah orders a fixed-term دَيْن to be written accurately, dictated by the liable party without diminishing anything, with witnesses: it is the section's two-sided ledger scene in full.

luna: This completes the debt-writing passage at 2:282: when a debtor is trusted, the one entrusted must “فَلْيُؤَدِّ الَّذِي اؤْتُمِنَ أَمَانَتَهُ,” fulfill the trust, making repayment a matter of fidelity. | terra: When no scribe is available, a رِهَٰنٌۭ مَّقْبُوضَةٌ secures the debt, while the entrusted party must discharge the trust and testimony must not be hidden.
terra: إِنَّ ٱلدِّينَ عِندَ ٱللَّهِ ٱلْإِسْلَٰمُ explicitly identifies dīn with islām, confirming the source dictionary's underlying sense of submission.

luna: This ayah describes gathering on a day without doubt and each soul being fully paid for what it earned, matching the section's due-account image. | terra: On the doubtless gathering day every soul is paid in full for what it earned without injustice, the section's closed account stated directly.
terra: God's dīn is set beside all in heaven and earth having أَسْلَمَ to Him willingly or unwillingly and returning to Him, making submission and final return the root beneath the account.
terra: A dīn other than islām will not be accepted and its seeker loses in the hereafter, joining submission now to the final balance.
terra: Righteousness is not attained until people spend from what they love, opposing the attachment to wealth that erases another's share.

luna: The section records the dictionary idiom كذب عليكم الحج as meaning that Hajj is incumbent; this ayah states the duty as “وَلِلَّهِ عَلَى النَّاسِ حِجُّ الْبَيْتِ,” pilgrimage to the House being due from people. | terra: The source's dictionary form كذب عليكم الحج means that pilgrimage “became due”; here وَلِلَّهِ عَلَى ٱلنَّاسِ حِجُّ ٱلْبَيْتِ states that very pilgrimage obligation, then names refusal as disbelief.
terra: After rejecting misappropriation by a prophet, the ayah says every soul will be paid in full for what it earned without wrong, linking entrusted property to final settlement.

luna: The section names withholding as the opposite of giving; this ayah condemns those who are “يَبْخَلُونَ” with what Allah gave them from His bounty, and says it will be placed around their necks. | terra: Those stingy with God's bounty should not call it good; what they withheld will be hung around their necks on resurrection, turning retention into a collectible liability.
terra: Orphans must receive their property, and guardians must not substitute bad for good or consume it, making the orphan's claim an enforceable entry.
terra: Guardians test orphans, deliver their property at maturity, avoid waste, and call witnesses; وَكَفَىٰ بِٱللَّهِ حَسِيبًا places the transfer under divine audit.
terra: When relatives, orphans, and needy people attend an estate division, they too must receive provision and kind speech, giving even the unassigned vulnerable attendee a share.

luna: The section's orphan is denied the care due to them; this ayah names the more specific abuse of consuming orphans' property unjustly and its punishment, showing the account attached to their rights. | terra: Consuming orphan property unjustly is described as eating fire, the final charge attached to the right that was taken rather than acknowledged.

luna: The section's dictionary form uses d-y-n for human debt as well as recompense; this inheritance rule says shares are determined after any bequest or debt is honored, placing an owed payment before distribution. | terra: Inheritance is distributed only after a bequest and دَيْن; an outstanding human debt remains a prior claim even at death.

luna: This repeats the debt-before-distribution rule in the case of spouses and siblings; it makes the section's literal debt-and-settlement sense concrete in another inheritance context. | terra: Repeated “after bequest or debt” clauses, together with the ban on injuring heirs, show a ledger of enforceable claims whose settlement precedes distribution.
terra: Mutual wealth may not be consumed falsely but only exchanged through trade by consent, marking the boundary between a valid transaction and seizure of another's right.
terra: The stingy, those who command stinginess, and those who conceal God's bounty display the same refusal to pass received benefit onward.

luna: The section's whole surah condemns giving only to be seen; this ayah describes people who spend wealth to show off before others, connecting display to the use of wealth. | terra: Those who spend to be seen by people while disbelieving in God and the Last Day join ostensible giving, display, and denial in one act.
terra: The question asks what harm would come from believing in God and the Last Day and spending from divine provision, directly reversing ostentatious spending without belief in 4:38.

luna: The section's account concerns what is owed and paid; this ayah says Allah does not wrong even an atom's weight and multiplies a good deed, defining the justice of settlement. | terra: God does not wrong even an atom's weight and multiplies a good deed, combining exact non-loss with generosity beyond the balance.
terra: Rendering trusts to their owners and judging justly gives the positive rule for recognizing another's haqq instead of taking it away.
terra: The best dīn belongs to one who أَسْلَمَ وَجْهَهُۥ لِلَّهِ while doing good, directly realizing the source dictionary's sense of obedient submission.
terra: The ruling demands justice for orphans and addresses withheld prescribed shares, directly reopening the orphan's erased line in the source ledger.
terra: A negotiated settlement between spouses is declared best while souls are prone to stinginess, placing reconciliation of rights directly against possessive withholding.

luna: The section's full surah exposes prayer performed carelessly and for display; this ayah describes hypocrites rising lazily for prayer and “يُرَاءُونَ النَّاسَ,” showing people. | terra: The hypocrites rise to prayer lazily and only to be seen, supplying the worship posture that can coexist with a false social account.
terra: Prayer, zakāt, belief in God, and belief in the Last Day occur together and receive a great reward, joining present payment to confidence in the final account.
terra: God approves islām as dīn after completing the dīn and favor, again making dīn an accepted order of submission rather than only the future day.
terra: The covenant combines prayer, zakāt, loyal obedience, and a good loan to God, assembling the same duties that the source's denier pulls apart.
terra: كَتَبَ رَبُّكُمْ عَلَىٰ نَفْسِهِ ٱلرَّحْمَةَ pictures God as writing mercy upon Himself, a boundary showing that the owner of the account freely binds Himself to mercy.
terra: All are returned to God, their true master; judgment belongs to Him and He is swiftest of reckoners, joining ownership, return, and account.
terra: وَءَاتُوا۟ حَقَّهُۥ يَوْمَ حَصَادِهِ requires the produce's due on harvest day, making provision carry another's payable right at the moment it arrives.
terra: The orphan's property, full measure and weight, and just speech appear together, joining protected right and accurate accounting.
terra: A straight dīn and the creed of Ibrahim name the ordered way whose obedience is unfolded in the next two ayat.
terra: Prayer, sacrifice, life, and death are all for God, showing how the dīn of 6:161 claims the whole account rather than a verbal affiliation.
terra: “No partner,” “I was commanded,” and being first of the submitters complete the obedience implicit in the section's root definition.
terra: The weighing that day is true, and heavy scales mark success; the account is an exact adjudication rather than an impression.
terra: Light scales disclose self-inflicted loss through rejected signs, linking denial to a deficit in the final balance.
terra: Calling on God with dīn made sincere is followed by return as He first created people, binding exclusive obedience to the return for settlement.
terra: Shuʿayb's command to give full measure and weight and not diminish people's goods restates the same two-party justice.
terra: The fifth of spoils is assigned in part to relatives, orphans, the needy, and travelers, turning received wealth into specified social shares.
terra: The ayah places dīn al-ḥaqq beside payment of jizyah and being brought low; whatever its legal context, it concretely joins a material due to dīn's submission sense developed in the source.
terra: Those who hoard gold and silver and do not spend it in God's way are warned of painful punishment, treating retained wealth as an outstanding liability.
terra: The hoard is heated and used to brand its owners, and they are told to taste what they stored, a material settlement of the withholding named in 9:34.

luna: The section's surah joins heedless prayer to withholding al-māʿūn; this ayah describes hypocrites who come to prayer lazily and spend only reluctantly, putting both failures together. | terra: Disbelief, lazy prayer, and unwilling expenditure are given together as the reason contributions are rejected, closely reproducing the source surah's linked failures.

luna: The section treats the poor's portion as a due; this ayah assigns zakāh to the poor and needy among named recipients, making distribution a defined obligation. | terra: The alms shares for the poor, needy, debtors, and other recipients are فَرِيضَةً مِّنَ ٱللَّهِ, making the gift an assigned due rather than dispensable kindness.

luna: This ayah's hypocrites close their hands, forget God, and command wrong while forbidding good; the closed hand is a specific parallel to the section's withholding of aid. | terra: The hypocrites forbid recognized good and close their hands, coupling social withholding with forgetfulness of God.

luna: This gives the counter-portrait to 9:67 and the section's refusals: believing men and women establish prayer, give zakāh, and obey God and the Messenger. | terra: Believing men and women command recognized good, establish prayer, give zakāt, and obey God and His messenger, reversing each relevant count in 9:67 and the source scene.
terra: Some covenant that if God gives bounty they will give charity and become righteous, establishing a promised payment from a received gift.
terra: When the bounty arrives, they become stingy and turn away, defaulting on the promise recorded in 9:75.
terra: Their broken promise and lying leave hypocrisy in their hearts until the meeting with God, carrying the unpaid covenant into its due date.
terra: Mockers deride both generous voluntary donors and believers who can find only their own effort; the ayah protects the smallest sincere contribution from being treated as worthless.
terra: God accepts repentance and takes charities, identifying the ultimate recipient and acknowledger of the payment made to human claimants.
terra: God “purchases” believers' lives and wealth for the Garden under a true promise, asking who better fulfills a covenant; obedience is cast as an exchange whose price will be paid.
terra: No expenditure, “small or great,” is made without being written to their credit for recompense, a direct positive version of the source's smallest unpaid due.
terra: Full measure and just weight are coupled with not depriving people of their things, making accurate accounting a social obligation.

luna: The section's dictionary form glosses dīn as obedience and submission; this ayah says judgment belongs to Allah and “ذَٰلِكَ الدِّينُ الْقَيِّمُ,” tying dīn to worshipful obedience. | terra: Judgment belongs only to God, who commands worship of Him alone; ذَٰلِكَ ٱلدِّينُ ٱلْقَيِّمُ joins governing judgment and exclusive obedience in dīn.
terra: دِينِ ٱلْمَلِكِ means the king's governing order here; this distinct Qur'anic use illuminates dīn as an authority under which conduct and liability are determined.

terra: The source's dictionary gloss of māʿūn as every benefit meets “what benefits people” remaining on earth here; the connection is indirect because this ayah contrasts enduring benefit with passing foam rather than alms.
terra: Those who do not answer their Lord would offer every earthly possession as ransom, yet theirs is the bad account; retained wealth cannot buy release.
terra: Those who fulfill what God commands to be joined and fear a bad account combine honored obligations with awareness of audit.
terra: Ibrahim asks forgiveness for believers يَوْمَ يَقُومُ ٱلْحِسَابُ, presenting the account's opening as a fixed event while seeking mercy within it.

luna: The section's repayment is an account coming due; this ayah says Allah will recompense every soul for what it earned and is swift in reckoning. | terra: God recompenses every soul for what it earned and is swift in account, identifying both payment and accountant.

luna: The section names the Day of Dīn as the endpoint of judgment; here Iblīs's curse is said to remain until “يَوْمِ الدِّينِ,” showing that the same day bounds a consequence. | terra: The curse upon Iblis lasts إِلَىٰ يَوْمِ ٱلدِّينِ, making that day the fixed endpoint at which a deferred judgment falls due.
terra: وَلَهُ ٱلدِّينُ وَاصِبًا assigns enduring dīn to God alone, supporting the source's “obedience” sense rather than only the name of a future day.

luna: This ayah pictures every soul arriving to argue for itself and being fully repaid for its deeds, a concrete scene of the account the section names. | terra: Every soul comes pleading for itself and is paid in full for what it did without wrong, joining personal liability and exact settlement.

luna: The section's debt ledger makes acts answerable; this ayah says each person's record is fastened to them and brought out on Resurrection Day. | terra: Each person's deeds are fastened to them and brought out on resurrection as an opened book, making the account inseparable from its debtor.

luna: The section imagines the account being settled; “اقْرَأْ كِتَابَكَ” tells the person to read their own book, which suffices as reckoner. | terra: “Read your book; yourself suffices today as reckoner against you” makes the denier confront and calculate the ledger personally.
terra: God extends عَطَآءِ رَبِّكَ to both groups and His gift is not restricted, opposing the human impulse to obstruct benefit.

luna: The section describes the miskīn's right as left unmentioned; this command says to give the miskīn and traveler their due, making the neglected share explicit. | terra: وَءَاتِ ذَا ٱلْقُرْبَىٰ حَقَّهُۥ وَٱلْمِسْكِينَ commands payment of the needy person's haqq, the opposite of removing that claim from the section's ledger.

luna: The section pictures the orphan pushed away and the poor person's need unacknowledged; this command says that when one must turn away from people seeking the Lord's mercy, one should address them gently.

luna: The section describes withholding the small benefit that is due; this ayah warns against keeping one's hand tied to the neck and against extending it completely, framing the use of wealth between stinginess and excess. | terra: The hand must be neither chained to the neck nor extended without limit, setting a measured boundary around the duty not to withhold.

luna: This continues the giving-and-rights passage at 17:26: it forbids approaching an orphan's property except in the best way, extending the section's due-paying image to guardianship of the vulnerable. | terra: The orphan's property may be approached only in the best manner, and covenants are answerable, combining a vulnerable claimant with an obligation that will be asked about.

luna: The section pictures an account ledger whose lines come due; here the book leaves nothing small or great unrecorded, and the wrongdoers fear what it contains. | terra: The placed book omits neither small nor great but enumerates it, and people find their deeds present: even the section's cheapest unpaid due remains on the ledger.

luna: The section describes a ledger and account; this ayah sets up just balances for Resurrection Day and says even a mustard seed's weight will be brought forward. | terra: Just scales are set for resurrection; even a mustard-seed weight is brought, and God suffices as reckoner, combining minute entry and exact settlement.
terra: Being named Muslims is followed by prayer, zakāt, and holding fast to God, bringing submission, worship, and the paid social due together.
luna: This opens the portrait completed by 23:2 and 23:4, calling successful the believers whose prayer is humble and who give zakāh—the opposite of the section's distracted prayer and withheld aid.
luna: Against the section's people who are heedless of their prayer, this ayah describes believers as humble in their prayers.
luna: This continues the believer portrait at 23:1–2 and names giving zakāh, the material response missing from the section's portrait.
terra: A book with God speaks truth and no one is wronged, making the record both complete and judicially exact.
luna: The section's ledger leads to judgment; this ayah says those whose scales are heavy are the successful ones.
luna: This gives the other side of 23:102: those whose scales are light have lost themselves, a contrary result in the measured account.
terra: People of means must not swear to stop giving relatives, the needy, and emigrants; the verse directly interrupts a chosen withholding of material aid.
terra: Tongues, hands, and feet testify to what people did on the day when God fully pays their true dīn in 24:25, supplying the evidence for that settlement.
terra: God will يُوَفِّيهِمُ ٱللَّهُ دِينَهُمُ ٱلْحَقَّ, fully paying people their true due; this is dīn in the section's concrete sense of recompense and payment.
terra: Commerce does not distract these people from remembrance, prayer, and zakāt because they fear a day when hearts and eyes overturn; ordinary trade remains under the final audit.
terra: God repays them for the best of their deeds and adds from bounty, while providing without account, completing the commercial and eschatological scene of 24:37.
terra: Prayer, zakāt, and obedience to the messenger form one command, making māʿūn's dictionary senses of obedience and zakāt converge in practice.
terra: The servants' spending is neither wasteful nor stingy but stands between them, clarifying that rejection of withholding does not erase proportion.

luna: The section's dīn dictionary form means judgment and recompense; Abraham hopes that God will forgive his sin “يَوْمَ الدِّينِ,” locating forgiveness within that accounting day. | terra: Ibrahim hopes for forgiveness of his error يَوْمَ ٱلدِّينِ, showing that the final settlement also admits the creditor's mercy.
terra: وَلَا تَبْخَسُوا۟ ٱلنَّاسَ أَشْيَآءَهُمْ forbids diminishing what belongs to people, the commercial form of erasing a claimant's line from the ledger.
terra: Prayer and zakāt are joined to certainty in the hereafter, the positive threefold relation opposed by negligent worship, withheld aid, and denial.
terra: Setting one's face to the upright dīn and God's created pattern presents dīn as the stable orientation of the whole person.
terra: Turning repentantly to God, fearing Him, establishing prayer, and avoiding association unfolds the obedience required by the upright dīn of 30:30.
terra: The relative, needy person, and traveler are each to receive their haqq; seeking God's face turns payment of their claim into worship.
terra: Usury meant to increase through people's wealth does not increase with God, whereas zakāt seeking His face is multiplied, correcting a false and a true account of gain.
terra: Prayer and zakāt again accompany certainty in the hereafter, linking payment of the present due to confidence in the final account.
terra: Even a mustard-seed weight hidden in rock, heaven, or earth is brought by God, so neither concealment nor smallness cancels a due entry.
terra: Whoever submits the face to God while doing good grasps the firm handhold, and the outcome of affairs is God's, linking yielded obedience to final disposition.
terra: Those who deny the Hour are answered that not an atom, nor anything smaller or greater, escapes God and all is in a clear book; denial cannot erase the smallest entry.
terra: Whatever people spend, God replaces it, and He is the best provider, answering fear that giving a benefit creates an unrepaid loss.
terra: Those who recite, pray, and spend secretly and openly hope for a trade that will never perish, casting worship and giving as one sound account.
terra: God pays their wages in full and adds from bounty, completing the nonperishing transaction of 35:29.
terra: God writes what people send ahead and the traces they leave, enumerating everything in a clear register; the account retains both act and consequence.
terra: When told to spend, the disbelievers refuse to feed those whom God could feed; their theological objection turns withholding food into denial, just as the source connects the two acts.
terra: Mouths are sealed while hands speak and feet testify to what was earned, preventing the liable party from denying the entries at audit.

luna: The section's Day of Dīn is the day the account is faced; the condemned exclaim “هَٰذَا يَوْمُ الدِّينِ” when they are raised. | terra: The raised deniers cry هَٰذَا يَوْمُ ٱلدِّينِ, recognizing the due day only when settlement begins.

luna: This completes 37:20 by identifying the day as “هَٰذَا يَوْمُ الْفَصْلِ,” the judgment the deniers had called false, clarifying what the section's account brings. | terra: “This is the day of separation which you used to deny” explains the recognition in 37:20 and turns prior denial into present judgment.
terra: The mockers demand their allotted share before the Day of Account, using the language of a payable portion while denying its appointed time.
terra: Severe punishment follows forgetting the Day of Account, showing that practical misrule grows from treating the audit as absent.
terra: هَٰذَا عَطَآؤُنَا فَٱمْنُنْ أَوْ أَمْسِكْ بِغَيْرِ حِسَابٍ combines gift, giving or holding back, and “without account,” marking sovereign largesse as a boundary to human default on a right.
terra: The same curse “until the Day of Recompense” again presents dīn as the terminal date of a judgment already entered.
terra: Worship with dīn made sincere for God presents religion as undivided obedience owed to its sole recipient.
terra: أَلَا لِلَّهِ ٱلدِّينُ ٱلْخَالِصُ states that pure dīn belongs to God, while false patrons expose diverted obedience.
luna: The section labels dīn as obedience; this ayah has the Prophet commanded to worship Allah sincerely in dīn, showing the obedience sense in a command to the speaker.
terra: The earth shines, the book is placed, witnesses are brought, and judgment is made in truth without injustice, staging the full audit.
terra: Every soul is paid in full for what it did, completing the book-and-witness scene of 39:69.

luna: This ayah states that every soul is repaid for what it earned and no one is wronged that day, making the section's debt-and-settlement image explicit. | terra: Every soul is recompensed that day for what it earned, with no injustice and swift account.
terra: Moses seeks refuge from every arrogant person who does not believe in the Day of Account, tying refusal of judgment to oppressive power.

luna: This is the warning completed by the next ayah, 41:7, which identifies the warned group as those withholding zakāh and disbelieving in the Hereafter; this ayah contributes the “woe” over that stance. | terra: The commanded declaration “I am only a human like you” ends in woe to the associators, identifying the addressees whom 41:7 then describes as withholding zakāt and denying the hereafter.

luna: The section links refusal of the final account to withholding what is due; this ayah joins “لَا يُؤْتُونَ الزَّكَاةَ” with being disbelievers in the Hereafter. | terra: لَا يُؤْتُونَ ٱلزَّكَوٰةَ and denial of the hereafter place nonpayment of the due and rejection of the final account in the same description.
terra: A wrong receives an equivalent recompense, while pardon and reconciliation earn a reward with God; exact balancing and merciful remission both belong within the account.

luna: The section's Day of Dīn closes the account; this ayah says every soul is recompensed for what it earned and none is wronged. | terra: Creation in truth culminates in every soul being recompensed for what it earned without wrong, the fair closure behind 45:28-29's books.
terra: Each community kneels and is called to its book to be recompensed for what it did, staging the public opening and settlement of the account.
terra: The divine book speaks truth because deeds were being transcribed, supplying the writing behind the summons in 45:28.
terra: People are invited to spend, but whoever is stingy is stingy only against the self; God is rich and they are poor, reversing their imagined creditor position.
terra: The two receivers seated at right and left record the human being, supplying the scribes for the final ledger.
terra: No word is uttered without a ready observer, so even the spoken denial belongs to the written account.
terra: مَّنَّاعٍۢ لِّلْخَيْرِ describes the obstinate doubter as one who keeps good back, joining withheld benefit to uncertainty about the final truth.
luna: The section treats dīn as the certain day of reckoning; this ayah says “إِنَّ الدِّينَ لَوَاقِعٌ,” that the judgment/recompense is surely coming.
terra: The scoffers ask أَيَّانَ يَوْمُ ٱلدِّينِ; their demand for its date is a form of resistance to the account's due day.
terra: The answer identifies the day on which they are tried over the fire, supplying the event behind their question in 51:12.
terra: “Taste your trial; this is what you sought to hasten” makes the scoffers confront the settlement they treated as remote.

luna: The section says the needy person's portion is a right; this ayah puts “حَقٌّ” in believers' wealth for “السَّائِلِ وَالْمَحْرُومِ,” the asker and deprived. | terra: A حَقٌّ لِّلسَّآئِلِ وَٱلْمَحْرُومِ in the righteous person's wealth makes the poor person's claim a booked right rather than a favor that may be withheld.
terra: كُلُّ ٱمْرِئٍۭ بِمَا كَسَبَ رَهِينٌ repeats the debt image: each person stands pledged as security for what was earned.
terra: Turning away introduces the person whose token giving and subsequent refusal are specified in 53:34.
terra: The person “gave a little and then stopped,” a precise enactment of conceding only a minimal benefit before withholding even that.
luna: The section's image makes what is owed come due; this ayah says a human being has only what they strove for, grounding the account in one's acts.
luna: This continues the effort-to-recompense passage at 53:39 by saying the effort will be seen, making the account's contents visible.
luna: This completes 53:39–40: the effort is repaid in full, a direct counterpart to the section's sense of dīn as recompense.
terra: وَكُلُّ شَىْءٍۢ فَعَلُوهُ فِى ٱلزُّبُرِ locates every act in written records, matching the source's account book rather than a forgotten favor.
terra: وَكُلُّ صَغِيرٍۢ وَكَبِيرٍۢ مُّسْتَطَرٌ makes explicit that the small as well as the great is inscribed, illuminating the withheld “small aid.”
terra: “Is the recompense for excellence anything but excellence?” expresses jazāʾ as answering return, the repayment sense that the source places under dīn.

luna: The section's dictionary form glosses the Day of Dīn as recompense; this ayah calls the punishment of the people of the left their provision on “يَوْمِ الدِّينِ.” | terra: “This is their hospitality on the Day of Recompense” turns the provision of the people of the left into a punitive payment rather than a sustaining gift.
terra: People are told to spend from what God has made them successors over, so the wealth from which aid is withheld is itself held on trust.
terra: The question “why do you not spend?” is answered by God's ultimate inheritance of heaven and earth, exposing withholding as a temporary holder's refusal.

luna: The section's debt dictionary branch meets the Qur'anic image of lending to God: “قَرْضًا حَسَنًا” is multiplied for the lender, giving generosity a promised return. | terra: مَّن ذَا ٱلَّذِى يُقْرِضُ ٱللَّهَ قَرْضًا حَسَنًا promises multiplication and a noble wage, reversing the source's default on a small due.

luna: The section's al-māʿūn dictionary form includes giving and zakāh; this ayah promises generous reward to men and women who give charity and lend Allah a good loan. | terra: Men and women who give charity are described as lending God a good loan which is multiplied, explicitly joining gift, debt, and recompense.
terra: Those who are stingy and command others to stinginess reproduce the communal refusal of aid, while God's self-sufficiency shows who truly owns the account.
terra: God has enumerated all their deeds though they forgot them, so human forgetfulness cannot close or alter the ledger.
terra: Charity is required before private consultation with the Messenger, making access carry a small payable social due before 58:13 mercifully waives it for those unable.
terra: After the waived requirement of pre-consultation charity, prayer, zakāt, and obedience remain due, clarifying mercy about one payment without canceling submission.
terra: Fay is assigned to relatives, orphans, the needy, and travelers so wealth does not circulate only among the rich, the structural opposite of accumulated unpaid claims.
terra: Those who prefer others despite their own need and are saved from the soul's stinginess embody the opposite direction from withholding al-māʿūn.
terra: The hypocrites command that support be withheld from those with the Messenger until they disperse, while the treasuries actually belong to God.
terra: Wealth and children must not distract from remembrance, since possession becomes loss when it obscures the account owed to God.
terra: “Spend from what We provided you” before death prevents the futile plea for delay in order to give charity once the payment period has closed.
terra: No soul receives delay when its term arrives, closing the deathbed wish in 63:10 to pay charity after the opportunity has ended.
terra: Spending what one can and being protected from the soul's stinginess prepares the “good loan” of 64:17 and reverses the source's refusal.

luna: This repeats the good-loan image connected to the section's debt-and-recompense relation: a loan to Allah is multiplied and forgiven. | terra: A good loan to God is multiplied and forgiven, so an apparent gift to another becomes a credit in the divine account.
terra: The question who could provide if God withheld His provision reverses scale: the person withholding a small benefit lives wholly on an unwithheld gift.
terra: مَنَّاعٍۢ لِّلْخَيْرِ names a habitual preventer of good, the direct moral posture carried by يَمْنَعُونَ in the source.

luna: The section imagines the account opened; the person given their book in the right hand says “هَاؤُمُ اقْرَءُوا كِتَابِيَهْ,” inviting others to read it. | terra: The person given the book in the right hand invites others to read it, the favorable opening of the same final ledger.

luna: This explains the confidence at 69:19: the speaker had expected to meet their account, matching the section's insistence that the ledger comes due. | terra: إِنِّى ظَنَنتُ أَنِّى مُلَٰقٍ حِسَابِيَهْ names the expectation of meeting one's account, the stance opposed to denying dīn.
luna: This continues the right-hand-book scene at 69:19–20, stating the person is in a pleasing life as the outcome of the account.
luna: This completes the outcome begun at 69:21 with a high garden, showing the reward beyond the account the section names.

luna: The section's denier rejects the coming account; this counterpart receives the book in the left hand and wishes it had not been given. | terra: The person given the book in the left hand wishes it had not been delivered, staging the debtor's failed attempt to avoid the record.

luna: This continues the left-hand-book scene at 69:25 with the regretful wish not to know the account, making denial's consequence visible. | terra: وَلَمْ أَدْرِ مَا حِسَابِيَهْ expresses dread of learning the account after the book has been handed over.
luna: This completes the regret at 69:25–26: the speaker wishes death had ended the matter, the opposite of the section's account continuing to its settlement.
terra: مَآ أَغْنَىٰ عَنِّى مَالِيَهْ shows that accumulated wealth cannot discharge the final liability, even though withheld wealth helped create it.
terra: Failure to believe in God is the first count immediately before failure to urge feeding the poor in 69:34, reproducing the source's bond between denial and an unpaid social due.

luna: The section says the denier does not even urge food for the poor; this ayah uses the same formulation, “وَلَا يَحُضُّ عَلَىٰ طَعَامِ الْمِسْكِينِ,” as the reason in the condemned person's portrait. | terra: وَلَا يَحُضُّ عَلَىٰ طَعَامِ ٱلْمِسْكِينِ is the direct parallel to the source's unmentioned poor person's food-share.
terra: The one who would not urge feeding the poor in 69:34 now has no food except a foul punitive food, an outcome shaped as a reversal of withheld nourishment.

luna: The section gathers the surah's refusal and neglect into a human portrait; this passage opens by calling humankind “هَلُوعًا,” then describes the behavior that the faithful exception reverses. | terra: إِنَّ ٱلْإِنسَٰنَ خُلِقَ هَلُوعًا introduces the grasping human type whose specific reaction to received good is withholding in 70:21.

luna: This continues the human portrait begun at 70:19 and completed by 70:21, describing the impatient response when evil touches a person; it supplies the other side of the unstable character whose response to good is withholding. | terra: Panic when harm touches the human being is the first reaction of the halūʿ character; paired with 70:21, it helps explain self-protective withholding.

luna: The section names withholding as the opposite of giving; this ayah says that when good touches a person, “مَنُوعًا” describes them as withholding, the same refusal made concrete. | terra: وَإِذَا مَسَّهُ ٱلْخَيْرُ مَنُوعًا depicts the withholding disposition named by يَمْنَعُونَ in 107:7.

luna: The section sets the surah's negligent worshippers against the exception in al-Maʿārij; this ayah begins that exception: “إِلَّا الْمُصَلِّينَ.” | terra: إِلَّا ٱلْمُصَلِّينَ opens the exception to the withholding human of 70:21, reversing the source's condemned worshippers.

luna: The section cites the prayerful exception to 107's distracted worshippers; this ayah specifies that they “دَائِمُونَ,” steadfastly maintain their prayer. | terra: Their persistence in prayer supplies the precise opposite of prayer that is neglected while its social due is withheld.

luna: The section says the poor person's share is not mentioned; here the faithful have “حَقٌّ مَّعْلُومٌ” in their wealth, a specified right rather than a discretionary favor. | terra: A حَقٌّ مَّعْلُومٌ in their wealth reverses the section's unpaid entry: assistance is recognized as a determinate right rather than optional largesse.

luna: The section says the poor person's share is omitted; this ayah assigns the known right to “السَّائِلِ وَالْمَحْرُومِ,” the asker and deprived person. | terra: لِّلسَّآئِلِ وَٱلْمَحْرُومِ identifies the two claimants whose known right is entered in 70:24, opposing the poor person's erased share in the source scene.

luna: The section connects denying dīn with denying the settled account; this ayah describes the faithful as those who “يُصَدِّقُونَ بِيَوْمِ الدِّينِ,” affirming that day. | terra: Those who يُصَدِّقُونَ بِيَوْمِ ٱلدِّينِ affirm the very account denied in 107:1, completing the explicit Meʿārij reversal developed in the source.

luna: This continues the faithful portrait after 70:26's affirmation of the Day of Dīn: they are “مُشْفِقُونَ” of their Lord's punishment, showing how belief in the account shapes conduct. | terra: Fear of the Lord's punishment immediately follows affirmation of the Day of Recompense, supplying the accountable stance behind the passage's prayer and recognized wealth-right.
luna: This completes the fear introduced at 70:27: no one is secure from the Lord's punishment. It gives the weight behind the section's account and recompense image.

luna: Continuing the same portrait after 70:26, this ayah says the faithful keep their trusts and covenants; it makes the section's debt and due-paying image an ethical obligation. | terra: Guarding trusts and covenants continues the portrait of those who affirm the Day of Recompense, adding faithful discharge of two-party obligations to the Meʿārij reversal.
luna: This continues the faithful portrait after its prayer, wealth-right, and dīn details at 70:22–26, specifying that they guard their prayers—the reverse of 107's heedlessness.

luna: This ayah joins the section's motifs in one context: establish prayer, give zakāh, and offer Allah “قَرْضًا حَسَنًا,” so worship and material due are both forms of obedience. | terra: Prayer, zakāt, and a good loan to God are commanded together, and whatever people send ahead they find with God as better and greater in reward.
terra: كُلُّ نَفْسٍۭ بِمَا كَسَبَتْ رَهِينَةٌ makes each soul collateral for its earnings, turning the section's debt image literal before the reckoning in 74:43-46.

luna: This is the question answered by 74:43–46: what brought the speakers to Saqar; the following answer names neglected prayer, feeding, and denial of the Day of Dīn, completing a scene of consequences. | terra: The question “What brought you into Saqar?” opens the itemized audit answered by neglected prayer, failure to feed the poor, and denial in 74:43-46.

luna: The section depicts inattentive prayer; in the answer about why they entered Saqar, these speakers say “لَمْ نَكُ مِنَ الْمُصَلِّينَ,” placing prayer among the neglected duties. | terra: لَمْ نَكُ مِنَ ٱلْمُصَلِّينَ is the first confessed unpaid item leading to denial of the Day of Recompense in 74:46.

luna: The section says the poor person's food is not urged; among the condemned speakers here, “لَمْ نَكُ نُطْعِمُ الْمِسْكِينَ” names failure to feed the poor as part of their account. | terra: لَمْ نَكُ نُطْعِمُ ٱلْمِسْكِينَ adds the poor person's unpaid share to the same confession that ends with 74:46's denial of dīn.

luna: The section's dictionary account culminates in a day people can deny; the speakers here confess “نُكَذِّبُ بِيَوْمِ الدِّينِ,” directly naming that denial. | terra: وَكُنَّا نُكَذِّبُ بِيَوْمِ ٱلدِّينِ gives the same denial, now confessed by those whose neglected prayer and feeding of the poor are itemized in 74:43-44.

luna: This completes the confession at 74:46: they say they persisted until certainty came, showing how the denial described in the section ends at death. | terra: The arrival of certainty closes the period in which the confessors could have prayed, fed, and affirmed the day; their account can no longer be amended.
terra: The human being is informed that day of what was sent ahead and left behind, a concise statement of both sides of the personal record.
terra: فَلَا صَدَّقَ وَلَا صَلَّىٰ joins failure to affirm with failure to pray, two liabilities the source and its Meʿārij parallel place in one account.
terra: وَلَٰكِن كَذَّبَ وَتَوَلَّىٰ answers 75:31 with denial and turning away, making rejected truth the stance behind neglected worship.

luna: The section's dictionary form connects dīn with obedience and its first image with an account that comes due; this ayah describes people who fulfill vows and fear a day's evil, joining obligation to the coming reckoning.

luna: Against the section's orphan and poor being denied care, this ayah says the righteous feed food to a needy person, an orphan, and a captive despite their own love of it. | terra: The righteous feed the needy, orphan, and captive despite their own love of the food, paying precisely the human claims neglected in the source.

luna: The section's whole surah condemns acts done for display; these feeders say they seek God's face and neither reward nor thanks from people, clarifying the motive opposite to showing off. | terra: They seek neither جَزَآءً nor thanks from recipients; the gift creates no human debt even though it remains in God's account.
terra: Fear of a grim day explains the unrequited giving in 76:8-9, opposing denial of the day that licenses withholding.
terra: The givers who sought no human recompense in 76:9 are told that this is their recompense and their effort is thanked, transferring repayment to God.
terra: وَكُلَّ شَىْءٍ أَحْصَيْنَٰهُ كِتَٰبًا states that everything has been counted in a written record.
terra: جَزَآءً مِّن رَّبِّكَ عَطَآءً حِسَابًا places recompense, gift, and measured sufficiency in a single phrase, the same semantic meeting developed between dīn and māʿūn.
terra: When the scrolls are spread open, the account that remained hidden during earthly exchange becomes publicly readable.

luna: The section quotes this divine question to the human who lives as if no account awaits: “مَا غَرَّكَ بِرَبِّكَ الْكَرِيمِ” asks what has deluded them about their generous Lord. | terra: The question what deceived the human being concerning the “generous Lord” names the giver whose bounty is answered by denial of dīn in 82:9.

luna: This answers the question in 82:6 about what could delude a person concerning the generous Lord: He created, formed, and proportioned them, making the question's appeal to divine care concrete. | terra: Creation, proportioning, and balancing begin to itemize the generous Lord's prior gifts before the denial charged in 82:9.

luna: Continuing the answer to 82:6, this ayah says God assembled the human being in whatever form He willed; the generosity questioned in the section is grounded in deliberate creation. | terra: Composition in whatever form God willed completes the received-benefit side of the account that the human then denies.

luna: The section's wording is “yukadhdhibu bi'l-din”; 82:9 says “تُكَذِّبُونَ بِالدِّينِ” of the deniers, an almost exact formulation that names the act at the center of 107:1. | terra: The wording كَلَّا بَلْ تُكَذِّبُونَ بِٱلدِّينِ repeats the section's charge almost exactly: the coming settlement itself is denied.

luna: The section imagines an account that will be opened; this ayah says guardians are assigned over people, introducing the record-keeping that the next verses specify. | terra: وَإِنَّ عَلَيْكُمْ لَحَٰفِظِينَ answers the denial of dīn in 82:9 with guardians over the deniers' still-open account.

luna: This completes 82:10's record-keeping scene: noble writers are appointed, a concrete ledger behind the section's account image. | terra: كِرَامًا كَٰتِبِينَ identifies the guardians as writers, making the record behind the section's ledger explicit.

luna: This completes the writing scene at 82:10–11 by saying the writers know what people do, identifying what enters the record the section says comes due. | terra: The writers know what people do, so denial cannot remove an act or withheld right from the account.

luna: After the recording in 82:10–12, this ayah gives the good-doers' outcome as bliss, one side of the recompense account developed by the section. | terra: The righteous are in bliss, the favorable side of the same written account kept by the scribes in 82:10-12.

luna: This completes 82:13's paired outcome by placing the wicked in the Fire, making the record's contrary recompense explicit. | terra: The wicked are in Hell, supplying the debtor class whose entry into it on the Day of Recompense is stated in 82:15.

luna: The section's dictionary form identifies the Day of Dīn with judgment and recompense; this ayah says the wicked enter it, “يَصْلَوْنَهَا يَوْمَ الدِّينِ,” describing the day in its punitive context. | terra: The wicked enter the fire يَوْمَ ٱلدِّينِ, giving the denied day its concrete settlement.

luna: This completes the punishment description at 82:15 by saying they will not be absent from it, giving the section's denied account an inescapable horizon. | terra: They cannot be absent from the fire, so the liable party cannot evade the due date named in 82:15.

luna: The section centers dīn as the day of recompense; this ayah asks what can make anyone know what the Day of Dīn is, introducing its gravity. | terra: وَمَآ أَدْرَىٰكَ مَا يَوْمُ ٱلدِّينِ magnifies the day whose reality the deniers try to remove from their account.

luna: This repeats and intensifies the question at 82:17 before the passage describes that day, underscoring the account that the section says is denied. | terra: The repeated question about the Day of Recompense prolongs the confrontation with the denied settlement.

luna: This completes 82:17–18: on that day no soul can do anything for another, and command belongs to Allah, specifying the finality of the account. | terra: No soul controls anything for another and command belongs to God that day, identifying the sole authority who closes every account.

luna: The section's ledger has unpaid rights and withheld aid; this ayah opens with a woe against those who give short measure, a direct scene of withholding what is due. | terra: Woe to the defrauders introduces a human account in which one party falsifies what is due, closely matching the source's ledger of denied rights.

luna: This specifies one side of the fraud in 83:1: they take full measure from other people, making their own due-counting exact while others' is not. | terra: The defrauders take their own measure in full, displaying the creditor's demand for exact payment while refusing reciprocity.

luna: This completes the measure fraud at 83:2: when they measure or weigh for others, they give less, a concrete reversal of fair settlement. | terra: When they owe measure or weight to others they cause loss, the same movement from denying the final account to withholding even a small human due.

luna: This follows the fraud in 83:1–3 by asking whether the defrauders think they will be raised, connecting short measure to the final account in the section. | terra: أَلَا يَظُنُّ أُولَٰٓئِكَ أَنَّهُم مَّبْعُوثُونَ asks whether dishonest account-keepers expect resurrection, explicitly joining the two ledgers.

luna: This completes 83:4 by naming the day of resurrection as a great day, giving the accounting warning its horizon. | terra: The “mighty day” is the due date that the defrauders' ordinary transactions should have made perceptible.

luna: The section's account day is a day when people answer before its owner; this ayah pictures all people standing before the Lord of the worlds. | terra: The people standing before the Lord of the worlds completes the transfer from a cheated measure to the final audit.

luna: The section imagines an open ledger; this ayah introduces the record of the wicked as “كِتَابَ الْفُجَّارِ” in Sijjīn. | terra: The wicked person's register is in Sijjīn, placing the dishonest accounting of 83:1-6 inside a larger written account.
luna: This continues the record passage at 83:7 by asking what Sijjīn is, focusing the reader on the place or register of the wicked mentioned there.
luna: This answers 83:8: Sijjīn is “كِتَابٌ مَّرْقُومٌ,” a written record, directly echoing the section's account ledger. | terra: كِتَٰبٌ مَّرْقُومٌ identifies that register as an inscribed book.

luna: This introduces the denial described in 83:11: on that day woe is for the deniers, joining corrupt measure to the fate of those who deny the account. | terra: Woe that day to the deniers announces the class whom 83:11 identifies specifically as denying the Day of Recompense.

luna: The section's central phrase is denial of dīn; this ayah explicitly calls the condemned “الَّذِينَ يُكَذِّبُونَ بِيَوْمِ الدِّينِ.” | terra: ٱلَّذِينَ يُكَذِّبُونَ بِيَوْمِ ٱلدِّينِ directly identifies denial of the settlement day, after 83:1-6 has staged dishonest human accounts.

luna: This continues 83:11's portrait of deniers of the Day of Dīn, specifying that only a transgressing sinner denies it; the section likewise joins denial of the account to social failure. | terra: Only a transgressing sinner denies that day, identifying moral trespass as the posture behind refusal of the final account.

luna: The section shows the denier's social failures; this passage sets out the record of the righteous in ʿIlliyyūn, the contrasting record of those who answer well. | terra: The righteous person's register in ʿIlliyyūn supplies the other side of the same final ledger.
luna: This continues the righteous-record passage begun at 83:18 by asking what ʿIlliyyūn is, directing attention to their register.

luna: This answers 83:19 with “كِتَابٌ مَّرْقُومٌ,” a written record, making explicit the other side of the section's account image. | terra: كِتَٰبٌ مَّرْقُومٌ again names an inscribed book, now recording the opposite outcome.

luna: This completes the register description at 83:18–20: those brought near witness it, showing the record is presented and attested. | terra: Those brought near witness the righteous register, contrasting an attested account with the denier's attempt to erase liability.

luna: The section's ledger is settled; this ayah says the person given their book in the right hand will face an easy reckoning. | terra: Receiving the book in the right hand begins the favorable settlement of the written account.

luna: This completes the right-hand-book outcome at 84:7 by specifying that the person is called to an easy account. | terra: فَسَوْفَ يُحَاسَبُ حِسَابًا يَسِيرًا promises an easy reckoning, showing that account need not mean denial of mercy.
luna: This completes that easy reckoning with the person returning joyfully to their family, the favorable outcome of an account answered well.

luna: The section's denier refuses the account; here the person given their book behind their back receives the opposite outcome from 84:7's right-hand recipient. | terra: Receiving the book behind one's back gives the opposite disposition of the same recorded liabilities.

luna: This continues the behind-the-back book scene at 84:10: the person calls for destruction, expressing the consequence of the account. | terra: The recipient calls for destruction when the unfavorable account is opened.
luna: This completes the outcome at 84:10–11 with burning fire, the contrary recompense to the easy account in 84:7–9. | terra: Entering the blaze is the settlement attached to that book.
terra: إِنَّ إِلَيْنَآ إِيَابَهُمْ locates everyone's return with the owner of the account.
terra: ثُمَّ إِنَّ عَلَيْنَا حِسَابَهُم makes their accounting God's own charge, directly stating who closes the ledger.

luna: The section pictures the orphan being thrust aside; this rebuke says “لَا تُكْرِمُونَ الْيَتِيمَ,” failing to honor the orphan, exposing the social neglect behind the image. | terra: بَل لَّا تُكْرِمُونَ ٱلْيَتِيمَ makes dishonoring the orphan a charge in the same account opened by the rejected orphan in the source.

luna: The section says no one urges the poor person's food; this ayah likewise reproaches people for not urging one another to feed the miskīn. | terra: وَلَا تَحَٰٓضُّونَ عَلَىٰ طَعَامِ ٱلْمِسْكِينِ directly repeats the failure to urge provision of the poor person's food.
terra: وَتَأْكُلُونَ ٱلتُّرَاثَ أَكْلًا لَّمًّا exposes indiscriminate consumption of inheritance, the taking of another's booked right behind the preceding neglect of orphan and poor.
terra: Intense love of wealth names the attachment that binds the passage's dishonored orphan, unfed poor person, and consumed inheritance.
terra: Freeing a neck is the first concrete payment on the steep path, replacing possessive power with release.

luna: The section names the poor person's missing food; this ayah describes feeding on a day of hunger as a steep moral passage. | terra: Feeding on a day of hunger reverses refusal to make the poor person's food available.

luna: The section's orphan is denied care; this ayah specifies feeding “يَتِيمًا ذَا مَقْرَبَةٍ,” an orphan of kin, as part of that passage. | terra: The orphan of near kin identifies one beneficiary of that costly feeding.

luna: The section's neglected miskīn is made visible here as “مِسْكِينًا ذَا مَتْرَبَةٍ,” a poor person in dust, completing the feeding scene begun in 90:14. | terra: The destitute person in misery identifies the other beneficiary, completing the scene opposed to denied small assistance.

luna: The section's refused due is reversed by the person who gives and is mindful; this ayah joins giving (أَعْطَىٰ) to fear of God and affirmation of the best reward. | terra: The one who gives and is mindful opens the exact opposite course from stinginess and withheld aid.

luna: This continues the giving portrait begun at 92:5: the person “صَدَّقَ بِالْحُسْنَىٰ” affirms the good, a counter-image to the section's denier of dīn. | terra: Believing in the best promise makes giving in 92:5 the positive counterpart of denial in 92:9.

luna: The giving and affirmation of 92:5–6 receive ease toward ease; this gives the section's account image a positive outcome for the one who answers rightly. | terra: God's promised ease answers the giver's affirmation, while 92:10 gives the denier the reverse path.

luna: Against the section's al-māʿūn as benefit and gift, this ayah describes one who is stingy and thinks himself self-sufficient, the posture behind withholding. | terra: The one who is stingy and considers himself self-sufficient supplies the inner posture of the person who refuses minor aid.

luna: This completes the reverse portrait begun at 92:8: the person denies the best reward, matching the section's denial of the account while refusing what is due. | terra: وَكَذَّبَ بِٱلْحُسْنَىٰ couples that stinginess with denial of the promised best outcome, echoing denial as the warrant for nonpayment.

luna: This completes the fate in 92:8–9: the withholding denier is eased toward hardship, a contrary outcome to the ease granted to the giver in 92:7. | terra: The stingy denier is eased toward hardship, giving the consequence of the two linked counts in 92:8-9.
terra: وَمَا يُغْنِى عَنْهُۥ مَالُهُۥٓ إِذَا تَرَدَّىٰ shows that the retained wealth cannot meet the final deficit it helped produce.
terra: The most mindful person is kept away from the fire, introducing the giver whose motive is explained in 92:18-20.
terra: The most mindful person gives wealth to purify himself, directly reversing the withholding and self-sufficiency of 92:8.
terra: No one has a favor with him to be repaid; the giver discharges human reciprocity and seeks recompense only from God.
terra: The giver seeks only the face of the Most High Lord, locating recompense with God rather than in a human return.
terra: The promise that the giver will be pleased closes the divine repayment of wealth given without a human debt.

luna: The section's orphan is pushed away; this command, “فَأَمَّا الْيَتِيمَ فَلَا تَقْهَرْ,” sets the direct boundary against overpowering or oppressing an orphan. | terra: فَأَمَّا ٱلْيَتِيمَ فَلَا تَقْهَرْ commands the opposite of driving the orphan away.
terra: وَأَمَّا ٱلسَّآئِلَ فَلَا تَنْهَرْ forbids repelling the petitioner, the interpersonal gesture that begins the withholding of even minor help.

luna: The section asks what it means to deny the settled account; after recalling human creation, this ayah asks “فَمَا يُكَذِّبُكَ بَعْدُ بِالدِّينِ,” what can make you deny the recompense now. | terra: فَمَا يُكَذِّبُكَ بَعْدُ بِٱلدِّينِ joins the section's verb of denial to dīn as the recompense still awaiting the human being.

luna: The section's dictionary form glosses dīn as obedience and its ending glosses al-māʿūn as obedience and zakāh; this ayah joins sincere worship, prayer, and zakāh as the commanded dīn. | terra: Sincere dīn, prayer, and zakāt are one commanded order here; ذَٰلِكَ دِينُ ٱلْقَيِّمَةِ makes explicit the obedience in which the source's first and last objects meet.

luna: The section's account makes even small dues matter; this ayah says whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it. | terra: An atom's weight of good will be seen, establishing that no useful gift is too small to enter the final account.

luna: This completes the accounting in 99:7 with the same visibility for an atom's weight of evil, so no small act escapes the reckoning. | terra: An atom's weight of evil will be seen, so withholding a seemingly trivial aid is not beneath the reckoning.
luna: The section's due-account has an outcome; this ayah says the one whose scales are heavy will have a pleasing life. | terra: Heavy scales introduce the favorable side of the final balance sheet.
luna: This completes 101:6 by naming the pleasing life as the heavy-scaled person's outcome, showing the result of the measure.

luna: This gives the contrary side of 101:6: the one whose scales are light faces an opposing result, like the denier whose due is refused in the section. | terra: Light scales introduce its losing side, where neglected small deeds have not disappeared.
luna: This completes the light-scale outcome at 101:8 by naming the abyss as the person's destination.
terra: People will be questioned that day about enjoyed bounty, making received benefit itself an accountable entry rather than ownerless surplus.
terra: The hoarder جَمَعَ مَالًا وَعَدَّدَهُ counts wealth while ignoring the account in which that wealth and its uses will be counted.
terra: Thinking wealth makes him immortal exposes why his private tally displaces the closing day of the true ledger.
terra: لَكُمْ دِينُكُمْ وَلِىَ دِينِ distinguishes two religious allegiances; it marks the confessional sense of dīn beside, but not identical with, recompense or debt.
